title: Tools are capabilities with a policy boundary
outcome: Design narrow tools and authorize every execution against current application state.
cue: A tool name describes a door. Policy decides who may open it.
version: Provider-neutral principles · Ruby 3.3 / Rails 7.2 lab · legacy Ruby 2.7 adaptation notes
useCase: Design narrow tools and authorize every execution against current application state.
benefits: A clear decision and a way to check it.
drawbacks: A broad “read database” tool can become a disclosure tool. Read-only is not the same as harmless or authorized.

trace.title: Narrow capability
trace.detail:
## Understand

A tool grants a possible capability to the host application, not an entitlement to every requested resource. Choose names and schemas that describe a specific operation.

Read_shipment_facts is easier to constrain than run_query or execute_code.

Bind the actor, tenant, role and request purpose outside model-supplied arguments. Validate IDs through current scoped data.

Recheck access at execution time, because a tool proposal can outlive the permission or record version it was based on.

Keep tools read-only until a product requirement justifies writes. Even read tools can reveal sensitive information or cause external effects, such as fetching a URL that logs access.

Restrict egress, output size, query cost and result fields. Tool annotations/descriptions are useful metadata; they do not enforce behavior.

trace.title: Follow one input
trace.detail:
Tool proposal → schema check → current actor resolution → scoped lookup → selected fields → bounded result. Test a foreign ID, revoked role, costly limit, unexpected field and URL argument.

Confirm forbidden text never reaches provider input.
